analysis.one_liner: Stops drug makers from switching patients to tweaked drug versions to block cheaper generic competition.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill unanimously in July 2024, but only after the product-hopping ban was stripped out, and the House never voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Drug companies sometimes keep a patent monopoly alive by pulling a drug off the market just as its patent expires and pushing patients to a slightly changed version covered by a new, later-expiring patent — a tactic called product hopping. This bill would make that illegal, let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the ban, and cap the number of patents a biologic drug maker can use to sue a biosimilar competitor in court. The Senate passed a version, but only after removing the product-hopping ban entirely, and the House never acted.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name and biologic drugs, along with the employers and insurers who help pay for them. By cutting off the product-hopping tactic and limiting patent pile-ons in court, cheaper generic and biosimilar versions could reach the market sooner, lowering prices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits product hopping — when a maker of a drug facing generic competition withdraws the original drug and steers patients to a modified version with a later-expiring patent — and lets the Federal Trade Commission enforce the prohibition.

When a biosimilar maker follows the required regulatory steps, the bill caps the patents a reference biologic maker can assert in an infringement lawsuit at 20, with no more than 10 of them being patents filed more than four years after the original product's approval.

The bill presumes product hopping occurred when a manufacturer, after learning the FDA received a generic application, withdraws the reference drug and sells a follow-on version, while allowing the manufacturer to rebut the presumption by showing its conduct was not intended to limit competition.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose the product-hopping tactic and their ability to bury biosimilar challengers under unlimited patent lawsuits, slowing expected revenue from extended monopolies. Patients could also see fewer incremental 'improved' versions of existing drugs.

drawbacks.text: The product-hopping presumption could sweep in legitimate product improvements — a genuinely better formulation or new use for an existing drug — forcing manufacturers into litigation to prove their intent, though they can rebut the presumption by showing their conduct was not meant to limit competition.

The patent cap is softer than it sounds: courts can raise the number of patents a biologic maker may assert for good cause, such as a material change in the biosimilar application, and method-of-treatment patents are exempt from the limit.
The version the Senate passed also added $1.8 billion to the Medicare Improvement Fund, spending unrelated to the bill's drug-competition purpose.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core idea targets a real and well-documented way drug prices stay high: extending monopolies by switching patients to near-identical versions of the same drug. The honest costs are the risk of catching legitimate drug improvements in the ban and added litigation for both sides. Weighing those, the bill as originally written would likely have been a net win for patients. But what actually passed the Senate was much weaker — the product-hopping ban, the bill's centerpiece, was stripped out, leaving only a capped-and-waivable patent limit — so even the version that advanced offered far less than advertised.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by unanimous consent in July 2024, but only after the product-hopping ban was removed, and the House then let the bill sit at the desk without ever voting on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 30, 2023, by Senator Cornyn and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary Committee reported the bill favorably without amendment on March 1, 2023, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar, but no floor action followed for over a year.
On July 11, 2024, the Senate took up the bill by unanimous consent and passed it with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

The version that passed the Senate contained only the limits on patents biologic makers can assert against biosimilar applicants, plus a $1.8 billion addition to the Medicare Improvement Fund — the product-hopping prohibition and FTC enforcement provisions from the original bill were gone.
The House received the bill on July 15, 2024, and held it at the desk; no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers came out ahead: the product-hopping ban that threatened their extended-monopoly playbook was stripped out before Senate passage, and the weakened remainder died in the House without a vote. Patients gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably without amendment out of committee and placed it on the Senate calendar in March 2023.

for.name: U.S. Senate
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill by unanimous consent on July 11, 2024, with an amended substitute text.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 15, 2024, held it at the desk, and never scheduled a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Manufacturers of reference drugs and biologics
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation restricting product hopping and biosimilar patent litigation, which would end a key method of extending drug monopolies.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsors split evenly, 4 Democrats and 4 Republicans; the Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent; the bill died in the Republican-controlled House without a vote.

industries.note: The original bill would have ended product hopping — pulling a drug as its patent nears expiry and steering patients to a tweaked version with a new patent — and capped the patent pile-ons used to delay biosimilar competition, both of which protect extended monopoly prices. The industry's interest in keeping these tools runs directly against patients seeking cheaper generics.

The bill limits how many patents a biologic maker can assert against a biosimilar applicant (20, including no more than 10 late-filed) and would have blocked product hopping, making it easier and cheaper to bring competing versions to market.
Earlier generic and biosimilar entry lowers the drug costs these payers cover, savings that flow through to premiums and patient cost-sharing.
